entry.content:

TRANSCRIPT

[Intro]
This is the SAP Developer News for October the 22nd, 2026.

[Shilpa]
Hello, SAP community. Devtoberfest 2026 is wrapped up after four weeks of learning, coding, and community activities. This year was another huge success with 2932 participants, out of which 62 people achieved a full score, meaning you completed each and every activity, including tagging the Kasimir cat every day. we call as Nerdvana thus qualifying for the grand prize drawing 10 lucky winners will receive an all -expense paid trip to SAP TechEd next year which is happening in Spain. Community also liked the fun side of Devtoberfest by posting your favorite pets in the Petoverfest, trying out the scavenger hunt and learning a bit of CAP and MCP in the snake & ladder game. Thanks to each one of you for participating, completing the challenge, and thus making the Devtoberfest a huge success. If you have ever missed any session or you want to re-watch, all the sessions are available in SAP Developer's YouTube channel, and then the information is also available in the Devtoberfest page in the Developer Center. Now, Devtoberfest has been wrapped up, and now the attention turns into SAP TechEd, which brings a new opportunity to learn and connect with the SAP developer community. See you in Berlin.

[Sheena]
We have two exciting updates for ABAP developers, ABAP Development Tools for Visual Studio Code version 1.2 and a major update to the ABAP Development Tools MCP server. Let's start with version 1.2 of the VS Code extension. This release introduces support for 23 additional ABAP object types, expanding the range of development artifacts you can create and manage directly in VS Code. It also brings several familiar ADT capabilities to VS Code, including the Transport Organizer, ABAP Feeds, Object Version History, SQL Notebooks for executing ABAP SQL queries, and Enhanced Activation Log, and HANA Source Code Search. There's also an improved experience for configuring system destinations, making it easier to connect to your ABAP system. The second highlight is a major update to the official ABAP Development Tools MCP Server which is bundled with ADT for Eclipse and VS Code. What makes this more exciting is that the MCP Server exposes ABAP Development Tools to AI agents through the model context protocol. With the new tools, it can work with command line AI clients such as Claude Code, Github Copilot, CLI, Codex, and OpenCode without depending on external file reading and editing tools. Some additional security features included are server switchoff by default, support for system allowlist, and object editing disabled by default. In short, ABAP development is becoming more flexible by bringing modern IDE experiences and AI agents closer to the about developers' everyday workflow. Check out the latest SAP Community blog post by Thomas Ritter for more details.

[DJ]
I'd like to draw your attention to a talk from one of our colleagues here at SAP, Guillaume Dellagustin at the InnerSource Summit 2026, which is a fully virtual around the world event taking place on Thursday, the 12th of November. He is a seasoned InnerSource Officer and his session is titled Inner Source in the Age of AI Challenges and Opportunities. Now, the questions he's raising in this talk are ones I suspect a lot of us are already wrestling with. Everyone can generate their own solutions now, so does that mean reuse is dead? Well, the bar for contributions to other projects has been lowered, of course, But what does that mean for people maintaining those projects? Guilherme will cover how AI can impact the collaboration style that InnerSource prescribes and share ideas on how to navigate this terrain. The summit is free to attend and runs continuously across every time zone. So wherever you are in the world, there's no excuse to miss it. Link is in the description.

entry.title: SAP BASIS HEALTH CHECK COCKPIT – ONE ABAP REPORT (NO SOLMAN / NO CALM)
entry.content:
Hello everyone,

It has been a long time since my last blog post. Work kept me busy, and honestly I only wanted to come back with something new, something that's not already on the community and that can really save time for others. I don't like repetitive work, and I don't like writing about things that already have ten blog posts. So here I am with a new one.

All my earlier blog posts were on Basis technical topics. This is my first blog post with ABAP . As a Basis person I'm not a full-time developer, but this need came straight from my daily work, so I decided to build it myself.

In this blog post we will learn:

  • How a Basis team can do active daily monitoring without SAP Solution Manager, SAP Cloud ALM or any other monitoring tool
  • How one ABAP report checks around 28 areas (application server, HANA DB, security, transport, interfaces and mail) in one run
  • How red / yellow / green colors help you see problems straight away
  • The prerequisites (2 Z-tables plus indexes) and the full source code, ready to copy

Here is the trailer, for full picture scroll down 🙃

THE PROBLEM – WHY I BUILT THIS:

Many landscapes, especially small and mid-size customers, do not have SolMan or CALM connected. Sometimes it's licence, sometimes the project is "still planned", sometimes nobody owns it. But the business still expects the Basis team to know about a problem before users call.

So what do we do? Every morning we open the same transactions, one by one:

SM51 → SM50 → SM66 → ST22 → SM37 → SM13 → SM12 → SP01 → SMLG → ST06 → DBACOCKPIT → STRUST → SCC4 → SE06 → STMS → SM58 → SMQ1 → SMQ2 → SOST …

and then the same again for the next system.

In my experience this takes [30–45] minutes per system if everything is fine, and more if something is not. After some days the eyes get used to the screens and small things get missed: one cancelled job, one SYSFAIL queue, a certificate expiring in 25 days. That is exactly what comes back later as a P1 ticket.

I wanted one screen that tells me what's wrong, how bad it is, and where to click to fix it.

WHAT THE REPORT DOES:

The report is ZBC_HEALTH_COCKPIT. In simple words:

  1. You pick a time window (since last run, today, yesterday, last N hours or a date/time range).
  2. The report runs all selected checks and gives each finding a severity.
  3. You get a summary ALV, one row per check, with the worst issues on top.
  4. Double-click a row → detail ALV with every finding for that check.
  5. Double-click a detail row → it jumps straight to the transaction (SM37, ST22, SMQ2, STRUST …), with authority check.
  6. Results are saved to history, and old runs are deleted automatically after N days (minimum 7).

SEVERITY AND COLOURS:

Severity Color Meaning
CRITICAL 🔴 RedAct now
HIGH🟠 OrangeAct today
WARNING🟡 YellowKeep an eye on it
INFO 🔵 BlueInformation only
OK🟢 GreenAll good
NOT CHECKED ⚪ GreyCheck could not run (authorization, connection…). Never shown as green.

That last point matters to me. If a check fails, it should never look green. A false green is worse than no monitoring at all.

CHECKS COVERED:

Area Checks
Application serverSM51 servers up/ping, SM50 free DIA/BTC/UPD WPs %, SM66 long-running WPs, ST22 dumps (with top runtime errors), SM37 cancelled jobs, SM13 update errors, SM12 old locks, spool number range %, SMLG logon group reachability/response, ST06 OS CPU / RAM / swap / disk I/O
Database (SAP HANA)Current and historical HANA alerts, data/log backup age (log_mode aware), memory vs allocation limit, CPU, disk volumes, services
Security & transportSSL certificate expiry (via standard report SSF_ALERT_CERTEXPIRE), SCC4 client open/closed, SE06 system/namespace change option, STMS imports with RC 4 / RC 8+
Interfaces & mailSM58 tRFC errors, SMQ1 / SMQ2 queues in error/stop, SOST failed/waiting mails

Every threshold (Warn / High / Critical) can be set on the selection screen, so you can save one variant for PRD and a different one for QAS/DEV.

1st screen of the report: where pre-select data will be there and also can be change based on your requirement keep last run reason as we have table too to store the data so not need to worry much but based on requirement you can select the options.

as there are multiple screens, every area param can be selected from each tab.

every tab have options, where you can change or update the values based on requirement and save it as variant, coz every landscape is having different requirement so instead of static i kept it dynamic so no code change needed only screen value is sufficient.

once executed it will show the top level ALV, where we can doubleclick on line item to see the details, if click on tcode it will route you tcode screen also

and in detail while click on that line item it will be easy to navigate and show the error information like below for each

every section and its details, a ease of life for monitoring team 😎

HOW THIS HELPS IN DAILY LIFE:

  • Time saving: my morning check went from [30–45] minutes to about [2–5] minutes per system. Run it, look at the red and orange rows, double-click, fix.
  • Better eye attention: we humans spot red much faster than a number in a column. Problems jump out of the screen.
  • Nothing gets skipped: on a busy day it's tempting to skip "just SOST" or "just STRUST". The report never skips.
  • Background job friendly: schedule it in SM36 with a variant (e.g. every 2–4 hours). With "Since last successful run" each run only looks at what's new since the previous one, so there's no overlap and no gap.
  • History for audits and handover: results stay in Z-tables, so you can show "what was the system status last Tuesday at 08:00".
  • Same standard for the whole team: a junior colleague and a senior colleague look at the same checks and the same thresholds.

A BIG THANK YOU:

This development would not have been possible without my friend i cannot disclose his/her name, who gave me access to his/her system to build and test it. A monitoring report can't be tested properly on a blank sandbox; you need real dumps, real jobs, a real HANA. Thank you, my friend, for the trust and the support. 🙏

I intentionally add his/her so no one in network also able to guess his/her name, it's a tricky part for my mates 😋

here is the code and other prerequisite ( in hindi we can say real masala 😅)

PRE-REQUISITES:

# Requirement
1SAP_BASIS 7.50 or higher (the code uses new Open SQL syntax and inline declarations). Built and tested on SAP S/4HANA on SAP HANA.
2Two Z-tables, ZBC_HC_RUN and ZBC_HC_RES: mandatory, see below
3Secondary indexes on ZBC_HC_RUN, so "since last run" and housekeeping stay fast
4SAPOSCOL running on all hosts (for the ST06 check)
5For the HANA checks, the DB user needs read access to SYS monitoring views and _SYS_STATISTICS (e.g. the MONITORING role). If your default connection user doesn't have it, create a DBCO connection with a monitoring user and enter it in the "HANA DB connection" field.
6Authorizations for the user / background job user to read the relevant admin data (SM50/SM51/SM12/ST22 etc.) and to call the jump-to transactions

TABLE 1: ZBC_HC_RUN (RUN HEADER)

INDEXES (FOR FASTER RUNS):

ZBC_HC_RES(primary key)MANDT, RUN_ID, SEQNODetail reads and deletes by RUN_ID already use the primary key, so no extra index is needed
 
 
CONCLUSION:
Proactive Basis monitoring does not require complex monitoring infrastructure. By consolidating critical checks into one ABAP report with direct drill-down capability, teams can **reduce daily check routines from 45 minutes to under 5 minutes**.
 
*All screenshots included in this blog post were created by me from a private test environment with all sensitive system identifiers, hostnames, and SIDs sanitized.*

entry.title: How to create a Custom migration object using LTMOM ( Upload resources to SAP TM )
entry.content:
Introduction

in this blog post we will create a new custom migration object to upload a resources into SAP transportation management TM, as there is no available migration object for resources master data we will explain how to build your own custom migration object to upload a resources into SAP TM.

So today we will see how to crate your own migration object to Upload a resource into SAP TM.

Blog content

  1. Prerequisites 
  2. Create a custom migration object using LTMOM
  3. Structure mapping
  4. Field mapping
  5. Testing
  6. Tips & Tricks

Prerequisites

Create a project using migrate my data application

Create a project for migrate data using staging table

Name the project, and select local sap s/4hana database schema

Select your package and go to step 3

Do not select any migration object, and click review

 

Confirm the warning that there is no migration object in the project

then create the project

Project will appear in the migration project list

Create a custom migration object using LTMOM

go to GUI interface and open Tcode: LTMOM, Select you migration project

Follow the below steps to create a custom

Write your migration object ID and select the target structure using function module

the function module used for creating a resource master data is: BAPI_RSSRVSCMB_SAVEMULTI2

also you need to select parameter for return: RETURN

select the target structure and check the fields that you need to fill, also take care of the mandatory fields, which you can check it in the transaction of creatin the resources itself

double click on the structure and check the fields that you need to upload

i recommend to collect all required fields then insert it in Excel sheet to be easy to manage and re-build it in the source structure

so i collected all the required field as per my need, collect each group of fields in a different tabs to be more structure, i used the below way

 

start build a source structure in LTMOM

click on source structure, right click then append structure to the lower level

create your own name, it is recommended to start the name with Z, then SAVE

Structure will appear here, in the right side we will start inserting the fields for that source structure

Click add and add your fields that you have collected in the excel sheet

make sure that each structure have its own KEY FIELD,

right click to build the second structure

 

make sure that key field are exist, in our case the resource number will be the KEY

also make sure that you linked this structure "Transportation" with the main structure "Header", this link can be done by below steps to link the KEY fields with Each others

Now our source structure is ready 

Structure mapping

the next step is to map the source structure to the target structure, drag and drop the structure to each other

 in my case i mapped the header structure to:

  • - logical system target structure because this structure are mandatory is to be mapped, you can later on create a fixed value for this field to exclude it from the upload template, but this is not our objective for now, we will map it and fill it to proceed further
  • header data structure
  • Application sign for TMS << this is very important.
  • change parameter structure << as it is mandatory also to be mapped, and if you did not do it, it will issue an error.

 also map the rest of structure to the target structure

Field mapping

the next step is to do the field mapping, our target is to map the fields in our source structure with the fields in the target structure.

you can do the mapping in automatically, but in our case we will do the mapping field by field, drag and drop the fields to link them each others.

we will do the same for all fields in our source structure

the tricky point here is you need to map the resource to change parameter filed as below

at the end, all your source structure should be mapped, and you will see all fields has a green indicator

click generate, and wait to see the generation status in the migration object

your migration object is ready and no error populated

Testing

next step is to test the upload, we will open our project again and start downloading the template

open migrate my data app, then select your project

 

you will see your migration object, and download the template in XML format.

 

here you can see your template, and your tabs ( Structure ) you have built in your custom migration object

Fill the data in the excel sheet and try to upload it.

upload your sheet by drag and drop your file

File uploaded successfully

Go back and click on prepare

you can check the status of the preparation in the monitoring screen

then the last step is to migrate your file

 

then check the status of the migration process in monitoring Log

you can check the message log, All success.

check also the data in the transaction itself > TCODE: /SCMTMS/RES01

you will see that all data are migrated successfully.

Tips & Tricks

  1. logical system and application sign fields are mandatory and you can set a default value for it and exclude it from the excel sheet.
  2. application sign should be " T " , the default value is " B " so it is mandatory to change it to " T " to be able to upload a resource master data for TM,  " T " means TMS ( Resources for TMS ), so i included this field in my source structure and excel sheet to be able to fill it with " T " Value.

Thanks

entry.title: Automating CERTRULE exception maintenance in S/4HANA for BTP apps
entry.content:
Introduction

In the previous blog I described how CERTRULE solves the problem of several e-mail addresses mapping to a single SAP user when BTP apps call the ABAP system with principal propagation. One rule covers everybody whose address is in SU01 and an exception list of explicit mappings covers the rest. That solution works. The effort to add the entries is cumbersome. When we moved from ECC to S/4HANA we had around 500 users to maintain as exceptions and it took our Basis colleagues more than 20 hours. This blog describes a much more efficient way to do it.

The two manual steps

Two steps have to be performed to maintain one entry in the exception list, typically Basis steps as they have the access to Cloud Connector and CERTRULE transaction in SAP.

  1. Open the Cloud Connector and generate a sample certificate with the e-mail address in the subject. 
  2. Open CERTRULE, import that certificate as an exception and assign the SAP user.

Screenshots to capture the steps:

Step one in the Cloud Connector. The subject pattern rule and the Create Sample Certificate action on its row.

The dialog asks for the e-mail address and generates the certificate.

Step two in CERTRULE (On SAP system). Import the certificate on the Explicit Mappings tab and assign the SAP user.

The certificate is read, CERTRULE shows the subject and the issuer, the status says the mapped e-mail does not exist, and the SAP user is required to be assigned. I'm adding default DEVELOPER SAP user in A4H.

One row in the exception list is created.

The work is in two systems (Cloud Connector and SAP), the certificate file is carried between them and a few minutes per address is required to add them.

Repeat for the next address. Both steps need a person with Cloud Connector administration and CERTRULE authorisations, which is why the work sits with Basis.

This makes it very time consuming. In our landscape, Basis team divided it amongst various Basis colleagues to make it possible to do it.

Questions on improving the process

To improve the process I investigated two things.

  1. Are both steps really essential.
  2. Can any of the steps be automated.

Initial automation thought

Initially I was thinking of a way to automate the generation of Cloud Connector certificates and then automate the import of the certificates in SAP. This will replicate the two stage process that we have to do manually.

However, I would not have admin access to the certificate via Cloud Connector keys to automate the generation of certificates. I gave up this approach as I realized it would not be possible.

I then changed my approach to investigate what SAP does when a certificate is imported in SAP. My theory was that the certificate is not technically essential. SAP is able to use certificate attributes to add the explicit mappings.

The first half covers the ABAP side: what CERTRULE actually stores, what the standard code behind the transaction does, which tables and APIs are involved and the issue I found around hashes.

The second half is the BTP side to make the solution work: A simple BTP app that reads a CSV file and calls a custom HTTP handler on SAP system to update the explicit mappings.

Landscape used for the test

The test ran on a local ABAP Platform trial in Docker with the Cloud Connector that comes with it. The BTP side is a trial subaccount on Cloud Foundry with a destination of proxy type OnPremise and authentication PrincipalPropagation. The identity provider is an Identity Authentication tenant.

The Cloud Connector issues a short lived certificate for every call from BTP with the subject CN=e-mail address,O=POC,C=AU and its own CA as issuer. CERTRULE maps the CN to the SU01 address with one rule. Every address that is not in SU01 needs an explicit mapping.

 

The browser knows an e-mail address. The token from XSUAA carries it. The Cloud Connector turns it into a certificate. CERTRULE turns the certificate into an SAP user. Only then does any ABAP code run. Nothing on the BTP side ever knows an SAP user name.

Step 1. Is the certificate essential

The first question was whether the certificate from the Cloud Connector is needed at all. The way to answer it is to see what CERTRULE does with it, so I debugged the standard code behind the transaction and traced what it reads and writes.

The explicit mappings tab in CERTRULE shows subject, issuer, user, creation date and creator. The old mapping table USREXTID has no creation date so the data cannot be there. SQL trace in ST05 while opening the tab shows the table. It is USRCERTMAP and it is read by class CL_CERTRULE_EXCEPTIONS in package SUSR_CERT.

The table has eight fields. The two key fields SUBJECTH and ISSUERH are hashes. The subject and the issuer are stored as text next to them but the key is the hash. That rules out a direct insert and it rules out SM30.

Step 2. The API behind the dialog

The import in the dialog reads the subject and the issuer off the certificate and hands those two strings to the SU01 identity framework. The certificate is only the carrier. Generating it in the Cloud Connector is required by the dialog to derive the attributes that end up in the SAP tables, but the certificate itself is not technically essential. That answers the first question and it opens the second one, because two strings can come from a file.

Class CL_CERTRULE_MIGRATION_UI proved useful in understanding this. That class shows how SAP itself creates a mapping without a certificate. It retrieves the users through the identity factory and adds a mapping with subject and issuer as strings.

cl_identity_factory=>retrieve_for_update(
  EXPORTING it_bname      = lt_bname
  IMPORTING et_node_root  = lt_identity
            eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ).

ls_certmap-subject     = lv_subject.
ls_certmap-issuer      = lv_issuer.
ls_certmap-change_mode = 'I'.
lr_identity->idref->if_identity_certmap~add_certmap(
  EXPORTING is_certmap    = ls_certmap
  IMPORTING eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ).

cl_identity_factory=>do_check( IMPORTING eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ev_rejected = lv_rejected ).
cl_identity_factory=>do_save( EXPORTING iv_update_task = abap_false
                              IMPORTING eo_msg_buffer = lo_msg ev_rejected = lv_rejected ).
COMMIT WORK AND WAIT.
cl_identity_factory=>cleanup( it_bname = lt_bname ).

The structure SUID_ST_NODE_CERTMAP has the hash fields and the string fields. The caller fills the strings and the framework computes the hashes on save. That is the whole trick. The certificate in the dialog is only there to read the two strings off it.

Step 3. It still didn't work

The first version passed the strings exactly as the explicit mappings tab shows them. CN=value,O=value,C=value without spaces. The rows appeared in the tab and looked identical to the rows created in the dialog. A sample certificate for one of them still came back with Mapped email does not exist.

The reason is in SE16. The issuer hash of the rows from the dialog was one value and the issuer hash of the rows from the API was another although the issuer text was the same. The identity API hashes the string it is given and the kernel hashes the distinguished name in its internal format. The migration class converts first with method CONVERT_DN of class CL_ABAP_X509_CERTIFICATE. Our strings are in LDAP format so the conversion is from CO_FORMAT_LDAP to CO_FORMAT_INTERN.

lv_subject = cl_abap_x509_certificate=>convert_dn(
  if_dn         = 'CN=testmassload@singhvikas.com,O=POC,C=AU'
  if_format_in  = cl_abap_x509_certificate=>co_format_ldap
  if_format_out = cl_abap_x509_certificate=>co_format_intern ).

After the conversion the hashes match and the explicit mappings tab shows the subject with a space after each comma which is how the internal format looks. The issuer is the CA that signs the Cloud Connector certificates not the Cloud Connector system certificate. Both values can be read from an existing mapping in the tab.

Step 4. The ABAP class

With the first question answered the second one is easy. A custom HTTP handler in the ABAP system takes the rows and runs the same API calls that the dialog runs, and a simple BTP app reads the CSV file and calls that handler. Everything above went into one class. LOAD takes the rows and the parameters and returns a log table.

It condenses the input, removes duplicates, marks an address that appears for two users as SKIPPED, checks each user with BAPI_USER_GET_DETAIL, skips addresses that equal the SU01 address because the rule covers them, converts subject and issuer, and runs the sequence from Step 2 with EXISTS for a mapping that is already there and WOULD ADD in test mode.

READ_MAPPINGS selects USRCERTMAP.

The class also implements IF_HTTP_EXTENSION so it can be called over HTTP. GET returns the current mappings as JSON. POST reads the rows from the JSON body, calls LOAD and returns the log as JSON.

METHOD if_http_extension~handle_request.
  DATA(lv_method) = server->request->get_header_field( '~request_method' ).

  IF lv_method = 'GET'.
    respond( io_server = server
             iv_json   = /ui2/cl_json=>serialize(
               data        = VALUE ty_list( user = sy-uname mappings = read_mappings( ) )
               pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-camel_case ) ).
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.

  DATA ls_req TYPE ty_request.
  /ui2/cl_json=>deserialize( EXPORTING json        = server->request->get_cdata( )
                                       pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-camel_case
                             CHANGING  data        = ls_req ).
  DATA(lt_log) = load( ls_req ).
  respond( io_server = server
           iv_json   = /ui2/cl_json=>serialize(
             data        = VALUE ty_out( user = sy-uname test = ls_req-test log = lt_log )
             pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-camel_case ) ).
ENDMETHOD.

The camel case setting of /UI2/CL_JSON maps a JSON field skipSu01 to the ABAP field SKIPSU01 without any mapping code. The user field in both answers is sy-uname. It is the proof that the call ran as the right person and the UI shows it in the header.

The class is registered in SICF under default_host/sap/bc with the class in the handler list and no logon data on the node. No logon data is the important setting. If a user were stored on the node every call would run as that user and principal propagation would be pointless. SICF service names are limited to 15 characters. The first attempt zpoc_certrule_load was cut to zpoc_certrule_l without a message. The node is zpoc_certmap.

A quick check before anything on BTP is built. Open https://host:50001/sap/bc/zpoc_certmap in a browser logged on to the ABAP system. It returns the current mappings as JSON. The Cloud Connector access control needs the same path on the mapping for the ABAP system.

Step 5. The CAP service

The CAP service has no entities. It declares one action and one function and forwards both to the ICF handler.

@path: 'loader'
@requires: 'Admin'
service LoaderService {
  action load(rows : many Row, prefix : String default 'CN=', suffix : String,
              issuer : String, skipSu01 : Boolean default true, test : Boolean default true)
    returns LoadResult;
  function mappings() returns MappingList;
}

The handler connects to the remote system declared in package.json, sends the rows in chunks of 200 and merges the logs.

this.on('load', async req => {
  const { rows = [], prefix, suffix, issuer, skipSu01, test } = req.data
  const a4h = await cds.connect.to('A4H')
  const result = { user: '', test: !!test, log: [] }
  for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i += 200) {
    const r = await a4h.send({ method: 'POST', path: '/zpoc_certmap',
      data: { prefix, suffix, issuer, skipSu01, test, rows: rows.slice(i, i + 200) } })
    result.user = r.user || result.user
    result.log.push(...(r.log || []))
  }
  return result
})

The remote system is three lines in package.json. Kind rest, the destination name and the base path.

"A4H": { "kind": "rest", "credentials": { "destination": "A4H_PP", "path": "/sap/bc" } }

The destination does the call to the backend system. Because it is OnPremise with PrincipalPropagation the SAP Cloud SDK takes the token of the logged on user, exchanges it at the destination service and routes the call through the connectivity service to the Cloud Connector. None of that is visible in the code. The three @SAP-cloud-sdk packages connectivity, http-client and resilience in package.json are what make it work. Without them the call fails with a bare fetch failed.

Step 6. The approuter and the scope

The approuter is the standard @SAP/approuter package. It logs the user on at XSUAA, checks the scope on each route and forwards. Two routes matter.

{ "source": "^/odata/(.*)$", "destination": "srv-api", "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "scope": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin", "csrfProtection": false },
{ "source": "^/(.*)$", "target": "$1", "localDir": "resources/loader",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa", "scope": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin" }

The first proxies the OData calls to the CAP service with the token forwarded. The second serves the UI page. Both need the scope Admin and the CAP service checks the same scope again with @requires. xs-security.json declares the scope, a role template and a role collection CERTRULE_Loader. After the deployment the role collection exists in the cockpit and is empty. Assigning the user is a manual step.

Step 7. The UI page

One HTML file with the UI5 controls created in JavaScript. A file uploader that reads the text file in the browser and splits it into rows, three input fields for prefix, suffix and issuer, a checkbox for skipping SU01 addresses, a table with the rows, a table with the log and a second tab with the current mappings. UI5 comes from the public CDN so there is no build step for the UI.

The input file is one line per mapping. The e-mail address and the SAP user separated by a semicolon. For us it comes from the old mapping table of the ECC system with the user and the address columns and nothing else.

newuser@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER
newuser2@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER
newuser3@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER

Step 8. Build and deploy

cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
mbt build
cf deploy mta_archives/certrule-loader_1.0.0.mtar

mta.yaml declares the service module, the router module and three service instances for XSUAA, destination and connectivity. The deploy creates the services, binds them and starts the two apps. cf apps shows the router URL.

Step 9. Load from the browser

For the one step path two more addresses were created in Identity Authentication, newuser2 and newuser3. The same kind of address as newuser, in no user master, so the only thing that can map them is an explicit entry.

The file has two lines.

newuser2@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER
newuser3@singhvikas.com;DEVELOPER

Open the router URL. The approuter redirects to the subaccount logon and from there to Identity Authentication.

The Mappings tab is the first thing to open. It shows the explicit mappings as read from USRCERTMAP through the whole chain and the header shows the ABAP user. If this tab fills nothing else can fail for a technical reason.

The Load tab. Choose the file and the two lines appear in the preview. Prefix, suffix and issuer are the values from the Cloud Connector subject pattern and CA.

Press Test run. Both lines come back as WOULD ADD and nothing is written yet. With the file from the old mapping table this is where EXISTS, RULE and SKIPPED show up and the file gets corrected before anything happens. The test run is the review of the file.

Press Load. The page asks for confirmation.

Two rows ADDED in a few seconds. When the identity framework rejects the save all rows turn into REJECTED with the first error message and nothing is written.

CERTRULE shows the three new rows together. newuser from the two manual steps at 21:38 and newuser2 and newuser3 from the app at 21:51. Same subject format, same issuer, same creator. 

Verification

The real proof is one logon with each address. newuser and newuser2 are in no user master, so the only thing that can make the call succeed is the mapping. Each address has a user in Identity Authentication with the e-mail address as login name and the status set to active, and the role collection of the small whoami app from the first post.

In a private browser window the app sends the logon to Identity Authentication. First newuser, the mapping created by hand in two steps.

The ABAP system answers DEVELOPER.

Then newuser2, the mapping written by the app from the file.

Same answer. The row written through the identity API from two strings in a file behaves exactly like the row created in the dialog from a certificate.

Summary

CERTRULE looks certificate based but what it stores is a pair of distinguished names per user. The identity framework takes those names as strings through IF_IDENTITY_CERTMAP and computes the hashes itself, so the certificate is not essential. It was only a carrier for two strings and the strings can come from a file. One ABAP class behind an HTTP handler does the load, a thin CAP service forwards to it and an approuter logs the person on. The exception list that took more than 20 hours of manual work for 500 users becomes one file and one upload that runs in a few minutes.

The real saving is in the cutover. Basis is the busiest team in that window and migrating the exception list was one more job that only they could do, entry by entry, at the point when they had the least time for it. With the loader the list is prepared ahead of time as a file, loaded in one step and checked with a test run before anything is written. The Basis team gets those hours back for the cutover work that cannot be handed to anyone else. The process becomes much more efficient and has fewer chances of error now that the manual steps are gone.

entry.title: onedevatlas is open: one connected graph for SAP developers
entry.content:
Today onedevatlas opens to everyone. It is one connected graph of what is built for SAP development, by SAP and by everyone else: packages, plugins, services, tools, MCP servers and skills, the problems they answer, the posts and talks that explain them, and the people who make them. One graph, read by people and by their agents.

Why it exists

Building has never been easier, and being found has never been harder. On 3 October the atlas listed 31 MCP servers for ABAP. Today it lists 42. Most of them are careful work, and many solve the same problem, because their makers could not see what was already there. Agents make it sharper: an agent knows what it was trained on and what the skills beside it describe, and the work of a freelancer, a partner or a customer team is rarely part of its answer.

The lists we have, for CAP, for UI5, for ABAP, are good and separate. What was missing is a view across the stacks, with SAP's work and the community's side by side, and a graph underneath that says how things relate.

 

A map drawn by capability

Every door, CAP, UI5, ABAP and BTP, and the smaller ones for SAP Commerce, SAP SuccessFactors and SAP Digital Manufacturing, has its own map. One hexagon is one capability, a concern a project has, and its colour says who is present: SAP, the community, both, or nobody yet. Open a tile and the capability page says what SAP ships, where that stops, and who else is present. Under a capability, use cases make the options comparable by the outcome they cover and the conditions under which they cover it, never by stars or downloads.

Behind the map is the graph itself, at /graph: select a node and its card says what it provides, who maintains it and what it depends on, each edge with one meaning.

The same answers for your agent

The hosted MCP server at https://onedevatlas.dev/mcp answers with the same facts the pages show. This exchange was recorded against the live server today: a question about letting a coding agent change ABAP in an on-premise system lands on a capability, then on an assessed use case with seven options, six covering it under conditions and one not known, and the four things that decide between them for your system.

Explore, and TechEd week

The third way in is a flight. Explore and Play is the same graph as a place: make an orb, design a ship and fly through the ecosystems. Until Sunday 1 November, midnight in Berlin, it is shared: sign in with GitHub, meet other pilots, play rock, paper, scissors (SAP style) and collect points for what you look at. Then the boards freeze, and the leaders stay in the atlas's history.

 

Take part

If your work is missing or something about it is wrong, open an issue. Anything about a person goes directly through the contact form. Maintainers can sign in and write a note on their own entry.

The full article explains the words the atlas uses and how to read a capability page, and its discussion is open.

See you at TechEd, or in flight. 🚀

entry.title: SAP Table to CDS Mapper - New Version thanks to AI-supported Development
entry.content:
TL;DR

I created a standalone HTML analysis that helps developers find possible CDS objects from a standard SAP table or table field. It combines direct field lineage with official successor hints and Cloudification Repository C1-release evidence. The snapshot covers 121,303 successfully analyzed CDS objects, 20,028 physical tables, and 1,647,510 direct field mappings and showed promising successors for over 2,000 tables that have no official successor at the moment.

Access the tool directly (thanks for the hint, Lars!) or Download the analysis package (ZIP). Extract it and open the HTML file; no SAP-system installation or additional service is required.
**This is a discovery accelerator, not an SAP replacement decision. The developer must validate business scope, semantics, authorizations, and performance for the intended use case.**

What is the issue here?

Finding a possible CDS object for a familiar SAP table is still more difficult than it should be. The Cloudification Repository, released object trees in ADT, and the SAP Business Accelerator Hub are valuable starting points. But successor information is not available for every table, and developers often start with a table and a field rather than the business-object vocabulary needed to find the right CDS object.

In my earlier post, How to find a CDS view for a classic Table in ABAP - Cheat Sheet, I described a pragmatic way to reverse-engineer direct table-to-CDS field relationships. This post takes the same idea one step further: I ran the analysis broadly on an SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01 system and created a portable report that lets a developer start from a standard table or a table field.

Important disclaimer: This is not an SAP tool and it is not a replacement-decision engine. It is an accelerator for discovering candidate CDS objects. A structural field mapping, a C1-release indicator, or even an official-successor indication does not prove semantic, functional, authorization, cardinality, filtering, or performance equivalence. The developer still has to validate that a candidate fits the concrete requirement.

Why an additional mapping is useful

The usual SAP tools rely heavily on maintained successor information. That is the strongest signal where it exists. However, not every classic table has a maintained successor. And an object can map relevant fields without being listed as a formal successor.

One useful example is T001L, the storage-location table. In the analyzed snapshot, it has no official-successor entry. Nevertheless, the report identifies I_StorageLocation as a C1-released candidate with direct mappings for 9 of the 22 persisted table fields. This is not a statement that I_StorageLocation replaces every T001L use case. It is a concrete, inspectable starting point for a developer who otherwise might not know where to look.

Using a deliberately cautious rule (no explicit official successor, a C1-release signal, at least three directly mapped fields, at least 30% direct coverage, excluding CUBE and value help views) the snapshot identifies 2,071 DB tables with a C1 released view as starting point. The Table explorer marks these as Good C1 candidate available and can filter for them. This is a prioritization signal only: it does not make the candidate an official successor or guarantee that it is suitable for a specific requirement.

For teams using Project Kernseife, I also provide a BF5 External classification import for these 2,071 additional successors. Choose not to overwrite existing classifications if you want to leave any existing custom classification untouched; those existing records will not be replaced by this import. If you choose overwrite instead, review the complete classification and preserve any existing successors that must remain. The classification is still only a curated discovery aid: validate that each CDS candidate fits the required business scope and works for the intended use case before relying on it.

What was analyzed

The snapshot was compiled in October 2026 on SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01. It contains metadata only; no business data was read or exported.

  • 130,647 CDS entities were placed in the extraction queue.
  • 121,303 CDS entities were analyzed successfully.
  • 20,028 physical base tables have persisted field-denominator metadata in the local report.
  • 1,647,510 non-calculated direct field-mapping rows are available for analysis.

* Not every available CDS object could be analyzed. This does not remove the value of the evidence that is present, but it means the report must not be interpreted as a complete catalog or a replacement decision.

How the data is compiled

The technical core is SAP class CL_DD_DDL_FIELD_TRACKER. For each analyzed CDS definition, it provides base-field information. The extractor keeps direct relationships between a CDS element and an underlying table field. Calculated elements are retained separately where useful, but they do not increase direct field coverage.

The process is broadly:

  1. Discover relevant standard CDS definitions in the analyzed system.
  2. Read direct CDS-element-to-base-table-field lineage.
  3. Persist physical-table field metadata so coverage can be calculated.
  4. Enrich CDS candidates with effective release, C1/cloud-usage, and official-successor evidence when the system provides it.
  5. Reverse the result: table and table field to candidate CDS entities and elements.
  6. Rank candidates: official successor first, then C1-released candidates, then direct field coverage.

I am especially grateful to Andreas Graeber. He shared the idea and solution with me before he open sourced and published CDS Analyser. Publishing it gave the community a practical implementation to inspect, reuse, and improve. This analysis builds on that generous contribution.

As mentioned in the title - this was done leveraging a new AI harness, so I tried "Hermes" for the first time (and quite liked it). I admit, it is mainly vibe-coded, so if you have ideas on how to improve this, feel free to take it from here!

How to use the report

The report has three views:

  • Use and limitations explains the purpose, evidence model, and validation boundary.
  • Table explorer lets a developer search a table, inspect the ranked candidate CDS objects, filter for official successors, C1-released candidates, or the cautious good-candidate signal, and expand a candidate to see the direct field mappings.
  • Overview provides aggregate coverage and concentration statistics for the snapshot.

You can identify possible successors in the Table explorer as shown in this example for T001L, which indicates I_StorageLocation as C1-released view that is worth diving into:

 

The field filter is especially useful for focused questions. For example, a developer can select EKKO, enter STCEG, and see only CDS candidates with a direct mapping for that field. The same filter updates field coverage. Candidate filters also update coverage: if the developer selects only C1-released candidates, fields that are not mapped by any C1 candidate are shown as gaps.

Evidence, not a guarantee

This distinction matters. A CDS object can deliberately model only part of a table's scope. The well-known repository-directory example of TADIR is useful here: a CDS object like the successor I_CUSTABAPOBJDIRECTORYENTRY may expose customer-created repository objects while intentionally excluding standard objects. A high mapping percentage can therefore still be wrong for a particular consumer.

For that reason, the report makes the evidence visible instead of turning it into a binary recommendation:

  • Official successor means that the system provides explicit successor evidence.
  • C1 released means that the snapshot found C1-release evidence for ABAP Cloud usage.
  • Coverage means direct structural field mapping, not business equivalence.
  • Good C1 candidate available is a cautious discovery filter for tables without official successor evidence; it is neither an SAP endorsement nor a replacement guarantee.
  • Unreleased candidates remain visible for investigation but are not presented as released API recommendations.

This aligns with the broader Clean Core principle: release information is important guidance, but developers still need to understand the intended API and validate that it meets their use case. The mapping helps to reduce the time spent searching; it does not remove engineering judgment.

Where this can help next

I see this primarily as a discovery aid for modernization work, custom-code remediation, and development teams that are moving away from direct table access. It can also support project-specific governance: once a team has validated suitable CDS objects for its relevant scenarios, those decisions can be maintained as explicit project rules rather than rediscovered repeatedly.

The result is provided as a standalone HTML analysis. Like the Excel sheet in the earlier post, it can be opened and used directly without installing anything in an SAP system or running an additional service. Refreshing the analysis for a later Feature Package Stack is still necessary, because available CDS content and release status can change.

If you use this kind of mapping, I would be interested in hearing which evidence you find most useful: official successors, C1 release, direct coverage, field-level lookup, or additional factors such as key fields and business-object metadata.

References

  • How to find a CDS view for a classic Table in ABAP - Cheat Sheet
  • agraeber/cdsanalyser
  • Cloudification Repository Viewer
  • Project Kernseife

entry.title: Dispute Resolution for Vendor Invoices: MCP Server App Designed in Hours, Not Developed in Months
entry.content:
From sales orders to supplier invoices

The second business AI app on our SAP ECC system works blocked supplier invoices, and it took one day to build.

In Part 1, Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server, we showed the Sales Representative Release Desk. Sales reps work blocked sales orders before the cancel date, and SAP suggests a decision for each order: release, extend, partial ship or cancel. The desk runs live on SAP ECC through Skybuffer AI, our ontology-based MCP server inside SAP.

This part takes the same approach to finance. The Invoice Dispute Desk resolves supplier invoices that SAP blocked for payment. This time the MCP server had no tools for invoice disputes yet, so the AI agent wrote them in ABAP, registered them in SAP and then built the app on top.

That is the advantage of the ontology approach: our MCP server describes SAP to the AI as business tools, not as OData services. When a use case needs more live SAP data or another action in SAP, the autonomous AI agent adds that tool to the server's registry. So apps like this are designed with the business unit in a workshop, in hours, not developed over weeks or months.

The problem: blocked invoices hold cash and burn discounts

Every blocked invoice is cash the treasury can't plan and, often, a cash discount that lapses while it waits.

Logistics invoice verification blocks a supplier invoice for payment when it doesn't match the purchase order and the goods receipt: a price above the order, more billed than received, goods that never arrived, or a manual hold. Duplicates add to the pile. Clearing each one means switching between MRBR, ME23N, MIGO, the vendor's email thread and a spreadsheet of who promised what.

On our demo system the board opened with seven blocked invoices worth 32,902.24 EUR. Of that, 6,976.00 EUR was in dispute, and 637.16 EUR of cash discount was at risk on six invoices that lose it within five days.

The app: one desk from diagnosis to release

The Invoice Dispute Desk puts every blocked invoice on one board, says what to do next, and lets the clerk do it with one tap and a confirmation.

The board

The board: tiles for cash, disputes and discounts, a stage rail and the worklist

Five tiles show what is at stake: invoices blocked for payment, the amount in dispute, the cash discount at risk, cases waiting on vendors, and invoices ready to release. A stage rail moves each invoice from New to Vendor contacted, Waiting, Ready to release and Done. Filters such as "Discount ≤ 5 days" put the money first.

Each row states the issue in plain words ("Wood Glue: 18.90 vs PO 18.00"), the days left for the cash discount, the case status and SAP's suggestion.

Diagnosis and a suggested next step

An invoice with SAP's suggestion and the three-way match per line

Opening an invoice shows the three-way match per line: ordered, received and billed quantity, PO price against billed price, and the amount over the order. A rules engine picks one next step and explains it with the amounts: release, request a credit memo, accept the price, post the goods receipt, reverse a duplicate or investigate.

For Halvorsen's wood glue it found a newer purchase order at the billed price, so it suggests accepting the price rather than fighting it.

Proof one tap away

Drill-down from the invoice into the purchase order and the prices on other orders

Every purchase order, goods receipt, invoice, vendor and material number is a link that opens live SAP data inside the drawer. Tapping the order shows three newer Halvorsen orders at 18.90 EUR, so the price change is visible before anyone accepts it.

Act, with a confirmation

Each action opens a short form and posts nothing until the clerk reviews and confirms:

  • release the payment block, as MRBR does
  • reverse the invoice, as MR8M does
  • accept the billed price: the PO price changes, then the invoice is released
  • post the vendor's credit memo or the goods receipt

A drafted vendor email, sent from SAP and recorded on the case

For a real dispute, the desk drafts the vendor email from a template per dispute type. It sends the email from SAP and moves the case to Vendor contacted, with a follow-up in three days.

Every step on record

The dispute case with owner and follow-up date, and its audit trail

Each disputed invoice gets a case in SAP with a reason, an owner, a follow-up date and an append-only audit trail of who did what. Resolved invoices move to Done, so the team sees what is left and what was settled.

How it was built in one day

Nobody opened a development project. The desk came out of one conversation between me and an AI assistant (Claude), connected to our SAP ECC system through Skybuffer AI.

One MCP server inside SAP builds the tools and runs the app

The assistant builds through the development tools, and the desk runs on the business tools they produce, both through the same server inside SAP.

Skybuffer AI also follows the SAP-endorsed architecture for AI agents: the same MCP server can be consumed through the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite on SAP BTP. That brings SAP's governance layer for AI agents on top, with authentication, rate limiting and observability.

The brief fit in a few lines: build a dispute resolution desk for vendor invoices in SAP ERD. Be creative: create ABAP classes and register them as tools where needed, refresh the MCP server, and create or clean the master and transaction data the demo needs.

From there Claude took over as my autonomous AI development agent, empowered by Skybuffer AI tools. ABAP Code Intelligence, one of those tools, guarded code integrity, so the new ABAP fits our existing code. The agent worked through SAP the way a developer would, only faster:

  1. Explore. It read the framework conventions and the existing tools in the MCP server, then the invoice landscape: RBKP, RSEG, EKBE and the blocked-invoice table RBKP_BLOCKED.
  2. Design. It proposed the toolset and the data model: a dispute case table, an audit trail table and a rules engine for the three-way match.
  3. Build. It created the tables and the ABAP classes through the MCP server's development tools, activated them and recorded them in a workbench transport.
  4. Register. It registered each class as an MCP tool, in a customizing transport, and refreshed the MCP server.
  5. Test live. It created four demo vendors with .example mailboxes, purchase orders, goods receipts and invoices, and tested every tool against them in SAP.
  6. Build the app. It built the desk on top of the tools and tested it end to end.

I reviewed the plan and the results. Every generated ABAP file header says so: requirements and review by me, design and implementation by Claude.

What the AI generated in SAP

The assistant generated nine MCP tools in ABAP, a rules engine and two tables.

X-ray of the desk: which generated tool sits behind each part of the screen

MCP tool What it does Writes to SAP

get_disputed_vendor_invoicesThe worklist: blocked invoices, open cases, totals and discount at riskno
get_vendor_invoice_dispute_detailOne invoice: three-way match per line, suggestion, case and audit trailno
manage_vendor_invoice_disputeOpens, updates, annotates and closes a dispute casecase tables only
post_vendor_invoicePosts an invoice or the vendor's credit memo, linked to the disputed invoicean invoice document, as MIRO
accept_invoice_priceChanges the PO price to the billed price, through BAPI_PO_CHANGEPO net price
release_blocked_vendor_invoiceRemoves the payment block, optionally moving the baseline date to keep the discountpayment block
reverse_vendor_invoiceReverses a duplicate or wrong invoice, through BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CANCELa reversal document
get_purchase_order_historyA PO with its history, its invoices and the prices of the same material on other ordersno
get_material_documentA goods receipt with quantities, values and reversalsno

Behind the tools sit the rules engine class /SKYBFR/CL_YAI_VIDSP, the case table /SKYBFR/YAIVIDC and the audit trail table /SKYBFR/YAIVIDL. The engine holds the three-way match, the rules and the open posting period. Both tables are also published as data sources, so the assistant can answer questions such as "which vendors take longest to reply?"

The desk also reuses tools the server already had: send_email, post_goods_receipt, get_vendor_details and get_material_stock. Everything sits in a workbench transport and a customizing transport, which go through normal change management.

Same pattern, second process

Both desks follow one pattern: a worklist of what SAP blocked, a diagnosis with a suggested decision, one-tap actions behind a confirmation, and a record of who did what. Only the business content changes.

  Sales Representative Release Desk (Part 1) Invoice Dispute Desk (Part 2)

ProcessSales orders on a delivery blockSupplier invoices blocked for payment
Who works itSales repsAccounts payable clerks
Deadline on screenThe order's cancel dateThe cash discount date
SAP suggestsRelease, extend, partial ship or cancel, from the ATP check and inbound receiptsRelease, credit memo, accept price, goods receipt, reverse or investigate, from the three-way match
Stages8 steps, from identify to follow upNew, vendor contacted, waiting, ready to release, done
Changes in SAPSales order changes through change_sales_orderRelease, reversal, PO price, credit memo, goods receipt, case log
Contact notes keptIn the page's shared storeIn SAP tables, with an audit trail
Partner emailDrafted for the rep to sendSent from SAP
MCP tools used713: 9 generated, 4 reused

The difference that matters: the Sales Representative Release Desk ran on tools the MCP server already had. The Invoice Dispute Desk needed new ones, and the AI built them in the same day.

Security and governance

The desk changes SAP only through tools that check the user's SAP authorizations, and only after the user confirms.

  • SAP authorizations apply. Each tool checks the authorizations of the person using it: M_RECH_BUK for invoice verification, M_BEST_EKO and M_BEST_EKG for purchase orders, M_MSEG_WMB for goods movements. With a direct connection, people sign in to the MCP server with their own SAP user through single sign-on.
  • Nothing posts without a confirmation. Every write opens a form and waits for Review and confirm. Postings go through standard SAP logic, such as BAPI_PO_CHANGE and BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CANCEL.
  • The page calls only what it declares. The desk lists the SAP tools it may use, and Claude asks each user before the first call.
  • No copy of SAP data. The desk reads live from SAP each time it opens. Cases and the audit trail are SAP tables.
  • Normal change management. Generated objects travel in transports, so they are reviewed and moved through the landscape like any other development.
  • Any model. Skybuffer AI works with Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or a self-hosted model. We built this desk with Claude.

What's next

Two processes, two desks, one MCP server: the next business app is a conversation away, and it can bring its own ABAP tools with it.

The 3-minute video shows the Invoice Dispute Desk on a phone, from the blocked board to the x-ray of the generated tools.

Which process should we take on next? Tell us in the comments. Questions about the ABAP side, the rules engine or the MCP server are welcome there too.

Links

  • Part 1: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server

entry.title: ALMathon 2026 - abat QA Cockpit: Ensure code quality in your Cloud ALM projects
entry.content:
Overview

The QA-Cockpit is an extension to SAP Cloud ALM that closes a gap in Cloud ALM around structured quality assurance for features before they go live.

In recent years quality assurance in SAP development has become increasingly important. It is essential to ensure aspects such as maintainability, a „Clean Core“ and security. For this reason, some customers have customized the Solution Manager for instance by implementing own statuses and individual checks. However, this is not possible with Cloud ALM, as the statuses and check routines are predefined. During ALMathon 2026, we bridged this gap by developing a comprehensive extension and adding features that are indispensable for modern development processes.

Developed during the SAP ALMathon

As part of the ALMathon, our litte team from the abat AG contributed a fully working prototype of the QA-Cockpit. The solution was ideated, designed and implemented during the hackathon, showing how SAP Cloud ALM can be extended with a dedicated quality-assurance layer that fits natively into the Cloud ALM experience

Why does the world need a QA-Cockpit?

SAP Cloud ALM gives teams strong feature and requirement management, but it does not provide a structured gate for quality sign-off, before a feature is released for testing or production. The situation quickly becomes complicated, when that feature involves several transports and transport objects that a QA reviewer must evaluate individually. The QA-Cockpit fills this gap by turning every Cloud ALM feature into a trackable „QA-Case“ with its own status, owner and audit trail. You can also view and click on the feature, project and requirement to which it belongs. By providing an AI review for the reviewer and the developer, even mandatory peer-reviews can be replaced. Additionally, the reviewer gains an overview that facilitates their work.

Challenges addressed

  • Transports, objects, check results and source code are stored in different systems, so the teams had to jump between systems to make their review.
  • The decisions (such as status changes and justifications) were not documented.
  • It was difficult to track who approved what and why.

Key features

  • Feature synchronisation: Each relevant feature automatically becomes a QA-Case and receives a clickable reference in Cloud ALM, allowing you to easily navigate to the QA-Cockpit
  • Transports, transport objects & transport checks: All technical artifacts underlying a feature are visible in one place, with automated checks surfaced directly in the QA-Case
  • AI review: An AI-generated review supports the reviewer by highlighting findings and summarizing the source code
  • Decision workflow: The actions „Approve“, „Reject“, „Not Relevant“ and „Assign“ move a QA-Case through a clearly defined status lifecycle
  • Comments & collaboration: Requester and reviewer can discuss directly in the QA-Case, with the entire history documented alongside
  • Audit log: Every status change and action is recorded for traceability
  • Native Cloud ALM look & feel: The application is based on SAP Fiori Elements and visually aligned with the Cloud ALM shell. This makes it appear as an integral part of Cloud ALM rather than a separate tool
  • Multilingual: The UI is available in English and German, switchable at any time

 

Inside QA-Cockpit

Overview QA-Cases

Below you can see a list of QA-cases, which were derived by the single features. This list can be used as backlog. A QA Team could use it to dispatch the cases in a regulary appointment.

Detailed view of QA-Case

If you click on a single case, wesee multiple details, which are linked to the corresponding QA entities as project, feature or requirement.

 

 

Architecture highlights

The architecture of QA-Cockpit leverages the following key components:

  • SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP): Powers the backend OData V4 service, the QA Case data model, and the decision/workflow actions.
  • SAP Fiori Elements (SAPUI5): Provides the List Report and Object Page UI for reviewing QA-Cases, transports, and AI findings.
  • SAP Cloud ALM APIs: Used to automatically synchronize features, transports, and transport objects into the QA-Cockpit.
  • AI review: Generates the pre-review findings shown on each QA-Case to support the reviewer.

What’s next

The QA-Cockpit started as a ALMathon build, but we see it as a starting point rather than a finished product, so we’re looking forward to testing it and getting better every day. We‘d love to hear from other SAP Cloud ALM  users for feedback, questions and collaboration opportunities. And if you want to know more about our product, please send us a message

Conclusion

Cloud ALM is a very good solution, which enables to implement requirements and enhance the standard solutions. Unfortunately, it's not possible to ensure code quality inside of the standard process. The QA-Cockpit fills this gap by providing many different checks as well to ensure approvals by quality managers.

The cockpit will optimize the development process including quality instead of only tracking implementation.

entry.title: ABAP Debugger Enhancement — Reloaded: Typed VALUE Statements and What's Changed Since 2019
entry.content:
This post was first published on LinkedIn. A German version is available on the T5 website.

The debugger often shows you exactly the data you need for a unit test — and then you end up retyping it by hand. DDVE (Debugger Data View Extension) saves you that step: one click, and you get a ready-to-paste VALUE statement. The latest update makes that statement typed and closes a few long-standing gaps — and since the last blog post in 2019, the community has contributed quite a bit as well.

How it works

DDVE adds a “Data for ABAP View” entry to the debugger in three places: the Services of the Tool menus of the table and structure tools, and the toolbar of the table's ALV display. The result is a syntactically correct, pretty-printed statement like this, ready to be copied into your test method:

" One click in the debugger turns the content of LT_FLIGHTS into:
DATA(lt_flights) = VALUE tt_flights(
  ( carrid = 'LH' connid = '0400' fldate = '20260115' price = '666.00' currency = 'EUR' )
  ( carrid = 'LH' connid = '0402' fldate = '20260116' price = '471.00' currency = 'EUR' )
  ( carrid = 'AA' connid = '0017' fldate = '20260117' price = '422.94' currency = 'USD' ) ).

 

The custom entry “Data for ABAP View” in the service menu of the table or structure view

The result popup with the generated, ready-to-paste VALUE statement

Under the hood, DDVE plugs into the standard debugger through three implicit enhancements — no modifications. All three hand over to the same pipeline: read the real data, resolve the type, render the VALUE statement, then format and show it.

Architecture overview: three implicit enhancements in the standard ABAP debugger hand over to the DDVE pipeline

 

New name, new home

If you know the tool from my earlier posts here on SAP Community from 2017 and 2019: it has since been refactored, extended and renamed, and it now lives in a new GitHub repository:

https://github.com/gepparta/abap_debugger_data_view_extension

I was also happy to find DDVE in the DSAG ABAP guide: the ABAP guidelines of the German-speaking SAP user group list it as the SAP GUI option for generating VALUE statements from debugger data.

All classes follow the ZCL_DDVE_* naming scheme. New in this update:

  1. Typed VALUE statements with inline declarations — DATA(flights) = VALUE flighttab( ... ) instead of an untyped #
  2. Robustness fixes for nested data in filtered exports, anonymous runtime types and empty tables and structures
  3. A refactored core with a much broader unit test suite

And since 2019, the community has contributed an ALV export that respects filters, hidden columns and sort order, .INCLUDE support and fixes for hashed tables — more on that below.

 

New in this update

1. Typed VALUE statements with inline declaration

Until now the generated statement looked like lt_flights = VALUE #( ... ) — fine as long as the target variable already exists and the compiler can infer the type. In a fresh unit test it usually can't.

Typed statements were an old feature request by Timo John — now they're here. DDVE resolves the variable's type from the debugger context and generates a self-contained inline declaration:

" DDIC type
DATA(table_of_flights) = VALUE flighttab( ( carrid = 'AA' connid = '0017' ) ).

" type declared inside a global class
DATA(item) = VALUE zcl_order=>ty_item( col1 = 1 ).

The interesting part is what counts as a usable type name. The debugger reports absolute type names such as \CLASS=ZCL_ORDER\TYPE=TY_ITEM or \PROGRAM=ZREP\TYPE=TY_LOCAL. Where no usable type or variable name can be derived — e.g. for a component path like LS_X-COMP — DDVE gracefully falls back to the classic untyped VALUE #( ... ), since DATA(...) with # would not compile. A new class ZCL_DDVE_TYPE_RESOLVER translates the debugger's type names into source-code-valid expressions:

Debugger type name Generated expression Why it works in a test

\TYPE=SFLIGHTsflightDDIC, visible everywhere
\CLASS=ZCL_X\TYPE=TY_Yzcl_x=>ty_ypublic always, private via LOCAL FRIENDS
\INTERFACE=ZIF_X\TYPE=TY_Yzif_x=>ty_yinterface components are public
\PROGRAM=ZREP\TYPE=TY_LOCALty_localtest include sits in the same program
\TYPE-POOL=ABAP\TYPE=ABAP_BOOLabap_booltype pools are global
procedure-local / generated typesfallback #not addressable from a test

2. Robustness fixes for the tricky cases

A couple of long-standing edge cases are gone:

  • Nested data in filtered exports — since the filter support from 2023 (see the community section below), nested tables and structures in the ALV export came out as placeholder texts like COL2 = `Structure: flat, not charlike` . When the debugger's ALV works on an internal copy of the table, DDVE now re-reads the real data and uses the ALV view only as a row and column mask — filters, hidden columns and sort order still apply, and nested data keeps its real values.
  • Anonymous runtime types — inline declared table types, OCCURS header lines, TYPE HANDLE structures — are now reconstructed from debugger metadata instead of silently producing no output popup at all.
  • Empty tables and structures produce a valid empty VALUE statement instead of broken output.

3. A refactored core with a broader test suite

The 2019 post already talked about single responsibility; this iteration went further. Rendering of VALUE expressions now lives in a dedicated class (ZCL_DDVE_VALUE_RENDERER) that owns the entire recursion for nested data, while the debugger facades for tables and structures only orchestrate. Output (CL_DEMO_OUTPUT), customizing access and pretty-printer creation are isolated behind their own small classes — which is precisely why the package now comes with a much broader ABAP Unit test suite, most of it mock-free.

Since 2019: contributions from the community

Between 2020 and 2023, several pull requests made it into the tool without ever getting a blog post of their own. If you still run the 2019 version, they are new for you as well.

What you see is what you get

Thanks to Daniel Wegner (@WegnerDan), the export respects what you see in the debugger's ALV:

  • Rows filtered out in the ALV are excluded from the generated statement.
  • Columns hidden in the ALV layout (no_out) are skipped.
  • The export follows the current ALV sort order.
  • The ALV's technical INDEX column no longer ends up in the generated statement.

So you can shape your test data visually in the ALV before exporting it — a surprisingly effective way to cut a 500-row production table down to the three rows that actually reproduce your bug.

More contributions

  • .INCLUDE structures — @juancarlosrodriguezf made sure that structures containing .INCLUDEs (e.g. a local type that includes T000 plus extra fields) are flattened correctly into the field catalog. Previously the included components were lost; the fix ships with its own unit test.
  • Hashed tables and performance — @sandraros contributed faster statement generation plus fixes for hashed tables and for tables with a component named INDEX.
  • Pretty printer and housekeeping — Andreas Kopp (@andkopp) fixed details in the pretty printer, and Christian Günter (@christianguenter2) brought the repository in line with the current abapGit format and fixed a syntax error.

Thanks to everyone who contributed! Two related posts here on SAP Community: Fork of ABAP Debugger Data View Extension tool and Speed up regression tests with the ABAP debugger, which uses the tool to create test data for regression tests.

A note on the built-in pretty printer

The 2019 post made quite a fuss about pretty printing the generated VALUE statement — including the option to plug in your own printer implementation via a pretty printer interface (today ZIF_DDVE_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER) and the customizing table ZTOP_DVE_CUST.

Honestly, this part has become less important: with ABAP Cleaner there is now an excellent open source formatter that aligns VALUE constructor expressions beautifully in ADT. So a perfectly fine workflow today is: export the raw statement with DDVE, paste it into your test method, and let ABAP Cleaner take care of the formatting.

The built-in pretty printers (and the customizing mechanism) are still there and still useful if you want a readable preview right in the SAP GUI popup — but if you are an ADT + ABAP Cleaner user, don't worry too much about this feature.

Migrating from the old installation

If you still run the original version (ZCL_OP_* classes), note that the enhancement implementations and the customizing table have the same names in both versions. Therefore:

  1. Export your ZTOP_DVE_CUST entries (if any).
  2. Uninstall the old package via abapGit (Uninstall/Purge).
  3. Pull the DDVE repository.
  4. Re-import your customizing and map the class names: ZCL_OP_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER → ZCL_DDVE_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER, ZCL_MAX_LINE_LENGTH_PP → ZCL_DDVE_MAX_LINE_LENGTH_PP.

Do not install both versions in parallel.

Prerequisites

NetWeaver ABAP 7.40 SP08 or higher.

How to install

All the coding is available here:

https://github.com/gepparta/abap_debugger_data_view_extension

Please use abapGit to get the coding into your system.

Pull requests and issues on GitHub are welcome.

Hands up: who has already used the extension? Or have you all moved on to ADT or VS Code and left the SAP GUI debugger behind – or is AI writing your unit tests by now anyway? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: Agentic AI for ABAP Development: What's New at SAP TechEd 2026
entry.content:
By Sonja Liénard, SVP, CPO of ABAP Platform, SAP SE

At SAP TechEd 2026, we are announcing innovations that take ABAP development further into the era of Agentic AI, building on everything we started at SAP TechEd 2025 and SAP Sapphire 2026. All these announcements point in the same direction: helping developers unlock intelligent automation, boost productivity, and build smarter enterprise solutions, regardless of where they are in their SAP journey.

Key highlights:

  • Three Agents on SAP Business AI Platform
  • SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment is now available on Alibaba Cloud
  • Major enhancements in the ABAP development tools 

Advancing the New Era of Agentic AI for ABAP Development

1. Agentic ABAP Development: Three AI Agents on SAP Business AI Platform

At SAP Sapphire 2026, we introduced our Custom Code Agents for SAP S/4HANA Migration. At SAP TechEd 2026, we are taking it further with three Agents on SAP Business AI Platform:

  • ABAP Custom Code Migration Agent
  • ABAP Clean Core Adaptation Agent
  • ABAP Application Modernization Agent

Custom Code Assistant (focus on ABAP)

These three AI agents are part of the Custom Code Assistant and work together to support the migration, adaptation, and modernization of ABAP custom code. The ABAP Custom Code Migration Agent helps accelerate custom code migration from SAP ECC to SAP S/4HANA. It can execute SAP S/4HANA readiness checks, apply deterministic quick fixes, use AI-based fixes with high confidence scores, and track all changes in transport requests. The ABAP Clean Core Adaptation Agent will help identify, and address ABAP Test Cockpit findings related to clean core compliance, while the ABAP Application Modernization Agent will support the modernization of legacy ABAP code toward ABAP Cloud development. Visit this document for more information about Agentic ABAP development.

For customers who are still on ECC and getting ready for migration, there is also a practical update to the Custom Code Migration App. You can now download ABAP Test Cockpit quick fix instructions and transfer them to your ECC system and apply automated SAP S/4HANA code adjustments before the technical conversion starts.

2. SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment: Expanding Global Reach

You may have noticed the new product name: SAP BTP ABAP environment is now SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment. Read more about the name change in this blog post.

SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment is now available on Alibaba Cloud, marking another milestone in its multi-hyperscaler strategy. China (Shanghai) is the first supported region on Alibaba Cloud, which becomes the fifth supported infrastructure provider alongside SAP Cloud Infrastructure, AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. For details about availability and supported service plans, read the dedicated Alibaba Cloud announcement blog post.

We are also planning an offering for SAP Sovereign Cloud for SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment, currently targeted for Q2 2027.

3. Latest Updates in ABAP development tools

At SAP TechEd 2026, we continue to make ABAP development more open, AI-enabled, and compatible with the tools developers already use every day. The latest updates to ABAP development tools for Eclipse and ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code bring significant advances for agentic development.

The official ABAP development tools MCP server received a major update, adding enhanced support for repository search, code editing, testing, transport handling, and integration with AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. For a detailed overview of the new capabilities and supported tools, read the dedicated blog post.

ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code version 1.2 adds support for 23 additional object types and introduces the first ABAP-specific views, including Transport Organizer, ABAP Feeds, Version History, SQL Notebooks, and HANA Source Code Search, further enhancing AI-enabled ABAP development in Visual Studio Code. Read the release blog post to explore all new features and improvements.

ABAP AI and ABAP IDE strategy join forces

 

What This Means for ABAP Developers

These announcements highlight SAP's continued investment in AI-assisted and agentic ABAP development. The AI agents support the migration, clean-core adaptation, and modernization of custom code for SAP S/4HANA. The availability of SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment on Alibaba Cloud marks another milestone in its multi-hyperscaler availability. The latest updates to the ABAP development tools MCP server and ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code bring new capabilities that help developers take advantage of AI-powered tools and modern development environments.

These innovations give ABAP developers more choice, more flexibility, and new ways to work with AI across the SAP development landscape. With AI handling more of the repetitive and time-consuming work, ABAP developers can focus on what creates real value: understanding the business, making good architectural decisions, and delivering solutions that last.

Sonja Liénard is Head of ABAP Platform at SAP SE. She leads the unit responsible for ABAP platform, ABAP Cloud, ABAP AI, and ABAP IDE strategy.
